item.title: Singapore and Johor Are Separated by a Narrow Strait Yet Combining Their Economic Strengths Is Much Harder Than Crossing the Causeway
item.description:
Working draft

This article sets out a hypothesis before primary research. It is published to invite scrutiny and will change as evidence comes in.

Stand on the waterfront in Johor Bahru after the evening rain and you can see Singapore’s high-rises across the strait.

The distance is short. The economic gap is not.

World Bank data puts Singapore’s 2025 GDP per person at about US$98,814 and Malaysia’s at US$13,125 (World Bank, 2026). The comparison is crude, but the difference matters. Singapore is a global centre for finance, trade, advanced manufacturing and regional corporate headquarters. It has capital, customers and skilled management, but little land and high operating costs. Johor, Malaysia’s southernmost state, offers more space, a large workforce and lower costs, with road links into Singapore through the Causeway and the Second Link.

item.title: Buying an Agency Without Destroying Its Value
item.description: An agency acquisition can look strong on paper. We look and believe that we see a good match of clients and sectors, specialist skills or IP that we need. We’ve worked out that we will benefit from shared costs and we might even have a shot at scale if things go well. So why does putting the firms together still damage the ties and working habits that made the deal look good in the first place? Why do so many acquisitions fail to deliver the promise? Why is it so difficult to make things work and why is it so frustrating to work in these post-acquisition businesses?
